analysis.one_liner: Bans children's products containing excessive cadmium, antimony, barium, or chromium.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2010 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal to make, sell, or give away any product intended for children 12 and younger if it contained cadmium, antimony, barium, or chromium above specific limits (for example, 75 parts per million for cadmium). These heavy metals can be toxic to children, and the bill enforced the ban using the Consumer Product Safety Commission's existing penalty system. It also preserved states' rights to set stricter rules and required the Commission to report to Congress on enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Children who wear, chew on, or play with inexpensive jewelry, toys, and other children's products would be protected from exposure to four toxic heavy metals. Parents would get a nationwide floor of protection, and states could keep or add tougher rules of their own.

how_it_helps.text: The bill banned the manufacture, sale, or distribution of any children's product containing more than set limits of antimony (60 ppm), barium (1,000 ppm), cadmium (75 ppm), or chromium (60 ppm) [S3].

It defined 'children's product' broadly to cover anything designed or intended for children 12 or younger that is sold at retail, using packaging, advertising, and common recognition to decide what counts [S3].
Violations would be treated as violations of the Federal Hazardous Substances Act and subject to its civil and criminal penalties, enforced by the Consumer Product Safety Commission [S3].
The bill explicitly preserved the power of states and cities to set or keep their own rules on these metals, rather than preempting them with a weaker federal standard [S3].
The Commission would have had to report to Congress annually on enforcement actions and penalties, and separately report on which other heavy metals should be banned [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and importers of children's products, especially makers of low-cost jewelry and trinkets that used these metals, would bear the cost of reformulating products, testing materials, and complying with the limits.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall hardest on small manufacturers and importers of inexpensive children's items, who would need to reformulate products and test materials against the new limits [S3].

The bill required the Consumer Product Safety Commission to create a new measurement standard within 90 days of enactment, a tight deadline for a technically complex task of making a mass-per-area standard statistically comparable to the parts-per-million method [S3].
The ban applied only to products manufactured 90 days after enactment, so products already on store shelves containing these metals could remain in circulation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit of keeping toxic heavy metals out of children's hands and mouths is substantial, particularly since cadmium was being used as a substitute for lead in cheap children's jewelry at the time. The main costs are testing and reformulation expenses for manufacturers, which are the normal costs of any product safety rule. The bill was a straightforward safety measure with few design flaws, though its short runway for the Commission's new testing standard was ambitious.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it; it died there when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Speier introduced the Toxic Metals Protection Act of 2010 on July 29, 2010 [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is where House bills on product safety normally begin [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; the full action history shows only the introduction and the referral [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired without becoming law [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and importers of children's products using cadmium, chromium, barium, or antimony avoided the cost of reformulating and testing their products. Children and parents gained nothing, since no federal limits on these metals in children's products were enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Manufacturers of children's products using these metals

for.name: Rep. Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its ban on toxic metals in children's products on July 29, 2010.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for product safety legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die when the Congress ended.

against.name: All 435 House members
against.what_they_did: No member besides the sponsor signed on as a cosponsor, and no member moved the bill out of committee or requested floor action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no recorded opposition votes and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan line ever formed; it simply never moved beyond its sponsor.

industries.industry: Children's product manufacturers and importers (toys, cheap jewelry, trinkets)
industries.note: The bill would have forced makers and importers of children's products to keep cadmium, antimony, barium, and chromium below set limits, requiring reformulation and testing. These metals had been used as low-cost substitutes in inexpensive children's jewelry, so the cost of compliance falls on the industry while the benefit goes to children.
The bill would have given the Commission new enforcement duties, penalty authority over the four metals, and a mandate to set a new measurement standard and report to Congress annually.
A legal limit on four heavy metals in children's products creates demand for testing services to prove compliance.
